_comment: Two lists, read by scripts/i18n-untranslated.mjs.
'accepted' suppresses a hit that a human read and judged correct as English IN THAT LANGUAGE.
Keyed by locale, key AND the exact value, the same convention as the diacritics baseline:
rewording a string retires its acceptance and the hit comes back, which is right, because the
judgement was about that sentence and not about that key forever.
Never bulk-accept. The default answer to a hit is to translate it, not to record it here.
'deliberate' is the opposite direction: keys that are English in all 46 locales ON PURPOSE.
The script checks they are STILL identical everywhere and complains if one drifts. Without that
check the next person to read the list 'corrects' them and the placeholder starts telling users
to paste an OAuth client id in translated Hungarian.
Deliberately NOT listed here, and left as ordinary hits, because the corpus contradicts the easy
assumption: 'protocol.discoverFileLuFtp' is translated in 40 of 46 locales and
'aeroShare.send.menu' in 44 of 46, so the handful matching English are misses, not coincidences,
even where the English happens to be valid in that language. A translator confirming a string is
already right costs nothing; baselining a real miss hides it forever.
'knownLeaks' is the same idea as the ratchet, for reference leaks. It is EMPTY: the one leak that
existed has been fixed. Entries are keyed by key AND value, so fixing or rewording
a string retires its entry automatically. Any leak not listed here fails the build outright.
THE RATCHET RULE, and it is a rule and not a convention. CI runs the detector with --max=<n>,
where n is the outstanding backlog. n comes DOWN in the same commit that does the translating,
never in a commit of its own, and it is never raised. A number lowered separately from the work
is a decorative counter: it stops measuring anything the moment the two can drift apart.
When n reaches 0 the flag becomes --strict and the ratchet is deleted.

deliberate.connection.internxtEmailPlaceholder: Email mask, not prose. It shows the SHAPE of the address the user types and all 46 locales already agree on it. The detector flags it only because 'your.email@example.com' parses as four words, one of them the function word 'your'. Confirmed by the Phase B translators: given the string and told to translate it, every one of the 46 returned it unchanged.
